04 CBTC Insights 
Beyond Landing: How I Understand the CBTC Ecosystem
The more I learned about CBTC, the less I saw it simply as an overseas technology park.
What interests me more is the system behind it: how a company moves from understanding an unfamiliar market, to making a decision, landing locally, connecting with the right resources, adapting to a different regulatory and business environment, and eventually becoming part of the local innovation ecosystem.
 When I place these services within a company's own development journey, I see them as a path that keeps moving forward:
DISCOVER → LAND → CONNECT → INNOVATE → GROW
01 · BEFORE LANDING, FIRST ASK WHY
 In an earlier conversation with Mr Liu, CBTC's Executive Director and General Manager, one point left a particularly strong impression on me:
 For technology companies going abroad, the first question is not how to do it, but how to define their own positioning.
Why are we going abroad?
 For different companies, entering Europe can mean very different things.
 Some are seeking new markets and customers; some want access to European universities, R&D and technology resources; some need industry partners; and others hope to establish a long-term European R&D or operational base.
 A company mainly looking for European customers will clearly need a different approach to establishing a local presence from a technology company seeking joint R&D opportunities.
 My understanding of cross-border incubation is therefore not:
 Take companies abroad first, then look for opportunities.
 Instead, it should be:
 First clarify what a company hopes to gain from internationalisation, then decide where to go and how to enter.
 The next issue that follows positioning is the information gap.
 A Chinese company considering Belgium for the first time will struggle to assess the local market solely through its existing experience. It needs to understand the industry landscape, policy direction, regional characteristics, potential partners and the differences between entry options.
 This is one reason I see CBTC's early-stage services as particularly valuable:
Market Research
Industry Information
Local Policies
Entry Strategy
Partner Search
 Ultimately, these activities are not about giving companies more information, but about:
Information Gap → Better Decisions
 Companies need to work towards answering:
Should we enter?
Where should we enter?
How should we enter?
 I increasingly feel that information is not an end in itself. The real value of early-stage services lies in reducing information asymmetry and helping companies find a direction that suits them.
02 · LANDING MEANS ADAPTATION
 Once the direction is clear, the questions quickly become practical rather than strategic.
 How should the company be established? How should personnel be arranged? How should contracts be signed? How should technology and intellectual property be protected? What requirements must products meet to enter Europe?
 Alongside positioning, this brings companies to another unavoidable keyword:
Compliance
 When an established technology company from China comes to Europe, it cannot simply replicate its existing operating model.
 It is entering a new:
Legal · Regulatory · Business · Cultural Environment
 My understanding of establishing a local presence therefore goes beyond registering a European company or finding an office.
Landing is not simply registration. It is adaptation.
 This is also why CBTC's one-stop services naturally extend to company establishment, local policies, legal and intellectual property matters, business matching, project management, government relations, and cultural and business training.
 These may appear to belong to different professional fields, but they all revolve around the same question:
 How can a company familiar with the Chinese environment gradually learn to operate in Europe?
 For me, this is also an interesting distinction between overseas technology incubation and conventional domestic incubation: alongside helping companies grow, it must help them adapt across markets.
03 · THE VALUE OF AN ECOSYSTEM IS WHO IT CONNECTS
 Learning about CBTC's partner network gave me a more concrete understanding of the word ecosystem.
 On the European side, CBTC connects with resources at several levels.
 In government and regional development, these include Wallonia, AWEX, in BW and Brabant wallon. AWEX's China Welcome Office has already established a presence at CBTC, providing local support to Chinese companies.
 In higher education and research, UCLouvain and Louvain-la-Neuve Science Park form a core, with connections extending to a broader Belgian university and research network that includes ULiège, ULB and KU Leuven.
 Industry and business networks add another layer. CBTC's partner network includes BioWin, Agoria, essenscia and Pôle MecaTech, representing life sciences, technology, chemicals and advanced manufacturing, alongside chambers and business networks such as the Belgian-Chinese Chamber of Commerce, BECI and VBO/FEB.
 On the Chinese side, the network CBTC has developed over time also extends to cities and innovation hubs including Beijing, Wuhan, Nanjing, Suzhou, Shanghai, Shenzhen, Chengdu and Taizhou.
 At this point in my research, however, I felt that the number of partners was not the most important conclusion.
 Because:
Having a network is not the same as creating value from it.
 What really matters is whether, when a company raises a specific need, the park can understand the issue and identify the kind of resource to connect it with next.
 Today, that may be market information;
 the next step may involve AWEX or a local government body;
 contractual, employment or regulatory questions may require lawyers, accountants and other professional teams;
 and the R&D stage may call for universities, laboratories, industry clusters or technology experts.
 My understanding of ecosystem value is therefore closer to:
Understand the Need → Find the Right Resource → Build the Connection → Keep It Moving
 A technology park does not need to be an expert in every field itself.
 Knowing what companies need at different stages, and bringing the right expertise into a project at the right time, is itself an important part of the park's ability to organise resources.
04 · FROM ONE-STOP SERVICE TO INNOVATION
 Following a company's development further, I do not see CBTC's one-stop services and its role as a technology park as two separate lines of business.
 They are more like different stages of the same company growth journey.
 When a company first enters Europe, its most urgent needs may concern market information, company establishment, personnel, premises and basic operations.
 As these matters stabilise, a technology company's questions often move forward:
 Are there suitable technology partners in Europe?
 Can we reach professors, laboratories or R&D teams in the relevant field?
 Can our technology find local applications?
 Could this lead to joint R&D, the commercialisation of research outcomes or industry collaboration?
 At this stage, the meaning of Technology Center begins to distinguish it from an ordinary business service centre.
 For a technology company, finding universities, laboratories or technology experts is only the first step. The greater challenge is finding specific points where its practical needs connect with research and technical capabilities.
 Companies may focus on products, markets and applications, while research teams may focus on technical approaches, research directions and the commercialisation of outcomes. Even when both sides want to collaborate, they still need to clarify the problem to solve, whose capabilities are the right match, and where collaboration can begin.
 My understanding of technology incubation therefore goes a step beyond connecting resources: it is not only about helping companies find whom to work with, but also about helping different innovation capabilities find what they can do together.
 CBTC describes its mission as building a Business and Scientific Ecosystem connecting Chinese and European companies. Its past practice reflects this approach: as early as 2019, CBTC facilitated a strategic cooperation agreement between Wuhan University, UCLouvain and CBTC. The park has also brought together European innovation projects through innovation and entrepreneurship competitions and cooperation forums, promoting China–Europe industry–academia–research collaboration.
 I therefore understand the overall process as follows:
 First, companies clarify their market and positioning through preliminary research;
 then establish a local operating foundation through landing services;
 next, enter government, professional and industry networks;
 technology companies can then connect further with universities, research, technology and talent;
 only then may they move from having a foothold in Europe to building their own capacity to develop there.
 This is how I understand:
DISCOVER → LAND → CONNECT → INNOVATE → GROW
 Different companies will also follow this path in different ways.
 CBTC's current companies include pharmaceutical and medical businesses such as Hubei Guangji Pharmaceuticals, H&Zedical and GMAX Bio, alongside ETSC in optoelectronics, Solar Parts in solar energy, and Nanjing Beite in environmental equipment.
 The research and regulatory resources needed by a biopharmaceutical company will clearly differ from those required by a company in optoelectronics, energy or environmental equipment.
 This is why I increasingly feel:
One-stop service does not mean one standard solution.
 It is more like:
 A service entry point that a company can return to over time, connecting it with different professional pathways according to its stage of development and specific needs.
05 · A MORE COMPLEX EUROPEAN MARKET
 Looking beyond the park itself, I feel that the European market CBTC faces today is already markedly different from the one it faced ten years ago.
 Europe still seeks to attract innovation, investment and high-tech companies. At the same time, it is more actively strengthening its industrial competitiveness, economic security, technological autonomy, and capacity for digital and green transformation.
 In recent years, the EU has introduced further policy measures relating to technological sovereignty, placing semiconductors, artificial intelligence, cloud computing and open-source technology at the heart of efforts to strengthen Europe's digital autonomy and industrial capabilities. Advanced-chip policies also increasingly emphasise supply-chain security, strategic industrial needs and reduced external dependence in critical areas.
 This reflects a practical shift:
 Europe still needs global innovation, while placing growing importance on the security, autonomy and long-term resilience of critical technologies, data, infrastructure and supply chains.
 These changes ultimately reach the level of business operations.
 AI companies need to understand new AI governance requirements; data-related businesses must consider data use, cross-border flows and security; advanced manufacturing and semiconductor companies may face supply-chain, technology-security and investment issues; and companies entering green industries must also address product, environmental, supply-chain and sustainability requirements.
 For a Chinese technology company entering Europe today, I believe market entry and compliance are becoming increasingly difficult to separate completely.
Market Entry is increasingly connected with Compliance Strategy.
 Companies still need to ask:
 “Is there a market for my product in Europe?”
 But at the same time, they increasingly need to consider in advance:
 “Are my company, personnel, technology, data, products and ways of collaborating suited to operating in Europe over the long term?”
 This is why I believe the government bodies, chambers of commerce, industry organisations, research institutions, and legal, tax and accounting professionals around CBTC have even greater practical relevance today.
 The park does not need to make final professional judgments in place of lawyers, accountants or technology experts.
 But if it can identify issues early in a company's development, help the company understand which professional field an issue belongs to, connect it with the right specialists, and bring their advice back into the company's actual projects and business context, many issues may be recognised before they become real obstacles.
 For companies, this is about more than avoiding risk.
 More positively, it can help them find paths for product adaptation, digitalisation, localisation and green transformation that meet the requirements of the European market.
 In other words:
Compliance should not only tell a company what it cannot do. Done well, it can also help a company understand how it can move forward.
 This is one aspect of cross-border enterprise services that I find particularly valuable today.
06 · FROM PRODUCT TO INDUSTRY TO BRAND
 This leads me to a further question: after Chinese technology companies enter Europe, what does it mean for them to truly establish themselves and grow?
 If they simply ship products made in China to Europe for sale, what they have achieved initially is product export.
 To develop here over the long term, however, they need to understand local customers, adapt to the rules, adjust their products, build teams and partnerships, and then reach further into technology, research and industry resources.
 The company's journey may therefore no longer be simply:
China → Product → Europe
 Instead, it may gradually extend into a longer path:
Product → Local Adaptation → Technology → Industry → Brand
 Product determines whether a company can enter the market;
 local adaptation determines whether it can stay;
 connections with technology and industry determine whether it can gradually become part of the local ecosystem;
 and what a brand ultimately accumulates is the long-term trust of customers, partners and the market.
 I like to summarise this shift in one phrase:
From Entering Europe to Becoming Part of Europe
 This does not mean requiring Chinese companies to become European companies. It means moving beyond selling products into Europe from outside, towards understanding the local environment, participating in local collaboration and building a foundation for long-term development.
 The same applies in the other direction.
 European technology companies seeking to enter China face similar information gaps, policy environments, partner-search and market-adaptation challenges. CBTC's value therefore lies not only in China → Europe, but also in Europe → China.
07 · RELATIONSHIP INFRASTRUCTURE
 After understanding this company development journey, I also began to look differently at CBTC's forums, business events, company visits and exchanges with government delegations.
 At first glance, these can easily be seen as event operations.
 Placed within the wider ecosystem, however, what an event leaves behind is often more than the event itself.
 An exchange with a government delegation may establish new institutional relationships;
 an industry forum may help companies that have never met discover one another;
 a technology matchmaking session may connect a company's needs with a suitable university or research team;
 and a company visit may become the next lead for investment attraction, investment or business cooperation.
 I therefore see these activities as a form of:
Relationship Infrastructure
Physical infrastructure gives companies a place to work. Relationship infrastructure gives companies a network to work with.
 Through innovation cooperation forums, innovation and entrepreneurship projects, and cooperation with governments and parks, CBTC has continuously connected resources on both sides. In essence, it has also been building this relationship network.
 Relationship infrastructure differs from physical infrastructure in one particular way:
 Its value often does not become fully visible on the day it is created.
 One meeting may simply introduce people; the next may begin an exchange of information; only later might a project emerge.
 In cross-border cooperation, this gradually accumulated trust, familiarity and ability to connect may be precisely what is hardest to replicate quickly.
08 · WHY CBTC MATTERS BEYOND THE PARK
 Finally, taking an even wider view, I believe CBTC has another significance that cannot be understood only in terms of serving an individual company.
 What it connects are two innovation and industrial systems, each with different strengths.
 For Chinese technology companies, Europe offers important research resources, high-level talent, industry clusters, mature markets and long-term brand value. For European companies and research institutions, China likewise offers a vast market, comprehensive industrial chains, manufacturing capabilities, and abundant opportunities for technology commercialisation and application.
 There is no shortage of potential demand for cooperation on either side.
 The real difficulty is that demand does not mean cooperation will happen naturally.
 There are still distances to bridge in language, institutions, information, regulatory environments, business practices and trust.
 I therefore understand CBTC's longer-term value as providing a local interface through which concrete cooperation can take place between two different market and innovation systems.
 This also helps me understand the two-way approach CBTC has consistently emphasised:
Going Global + Bringing In
 Going global means helping Chinese technology companies understand Europe, establish a local operating foundation, and gradually enter European industry, research and professional networks.
 Bringing in means connecting European companies, technologies, research projects and innovation resources with China's market, industrial parks and practical cooperation needs.
 This two-way approach is not simply about setting up a service point in China and another in Europe. It involves continually connecting local governments, innovation parks, universities and research institutions, industry organisations, professional bodies and companies on both sides.
 To me, a two-way China–Europe platform therefore resembles an expanding network: resources on the two sides are not simply exchanged, but brought together where they can connect meaningfully within specific companies and projects.
 From a broader perspective, this also gives CBTC a significance beyond operating an individual park.
 It supports the internationalisation of Chinese technology companies while providing a channel for European innovation resources to enter the Chinese market. It meets companies' practical needs for going global while also contributing to bringing in resources and to China–Europe cooperation in technology, trade and business. From overseas economic and trade cooperation under the Belt and Road framework to being described as a successful example of China–Belgium cooperation, this two-way character has run throughout CBTC's development.
 I believe, however, that its strategic value must ultimately be realised through specific cooperation:
 A company, a laboratory, a technology, a partner, an industrial project, or a business relationship that can continue developing over the long term.
 Especially today, with technology, industry and regulatory environments between China and Europe becoming more complex, I feel that a platform able to understand both environments, connect specific resources and help cooperation keep moving forward will become even more meaningful.
 Not by eliminating differences or bypassing rules.
 But by:
Understand the differences. Connect the right resources. Find workable paths for cooperation.
MY UNDERSTANDING
 Returning to the beginning, if I were asked how I understand CBTC now, I would not first think of a technology park building, or only of one-stop enterprise services.
 I would prefer to understand it through a company's actual journey.
 When companies first consider internationalisation, they need to reduce information gaps, understand the market and clarify why they are going abroad. After deciding to enter, they need to adapt to new legal, regulatory and business environments. When they encounter issues they cannot resolve alone, they need government bodies, chambers of commerce, professional institutions and industry partners. Technology companies may then go further in connecting with universities, research, technology and talent.
 These stages may look very different, but together they address the same question:
 How can a company move, step by step, from wanting to enter another market to being genuinely able to develop there?
 In this process, CBTC connects more than space and services. It also connects information, expertise, technology, institutions, relationships between people, and the trust that takes time to build in cross-border cooperation.
 I therefore now see CBTC as a long-term interface connecting China and Europe: helping companies clarify their direction, adapt to a new environment, and find the right people and resources, while turning cross-border cooperation that begins as ideas and opportunities into projects that can actually move forward.
 This is also precisely why I am enthusiastic about this kind of work. Many valuable collaborations begin with a need, a conversation, or even an idea that is not yet clear. Understanding it, connecting the right people and resources, and helping it gradually take shape is meaningful work in itself.
